textbookText: Procedure: i. Briefly introduce the topic of cellular structures. ii. Explain the importance of understanding the different parts of a cell and their functions. iii. Divide the class into small groups, each group consisting of 5-7 students. iv. Assign each group to a bench. v. Provide a pool of cheat slips with names of various cellular structures. vi. Ask each group to randomly select one cheat slip to determine which cellular structure they will work on. vii. Each group receives chart paper and color pens/pencils. viii. Instruct each group to: − draw an accurate and detailed image of their assigned cellular structure. − label all parts of the structure. − draw a table to list the features and functions of the structure. ix. Each group presents their drawing and table and explains features to the class. x. Summarize the key points about each cellular structure discussed. xi. Assign homework where students write a short report on any one cellular structure of their choice, including an illustration and a detailed explanation of its features and functions. xii. Briefly explain the importance of cellular structures. xiii. Groups present their work to the class. xiv. Recap key points and discuss the structures. xv. Give them assignment - 'Write a report on one cellular structure with illustration, features and functions'.

16. CELL INCLUSIONS Due to metabolic activities in the cell, several non-living substances are produced. The metabolically inactive non-living substances such as proteins, amino compounds, starch grains, essential oils, latex, mineral crystals, cellulose, inulin, sugars, fats, oils, pigment, enzymes, etc.

present in the cytoplasm of the cell are known as cell inclusions or deutoplasmic bodies or ergastic bodies.
Cell inclusions can be divided into three categories: 1. Reserve materials 2. Secretory materials 3. Excretory materials
1. Reserve materials The metabolic products stored in plant cells form the reserve food of the plant. They are either nitrogenous or non-nitrogenous and may remain in solid form or liquid form.

a. Nitrogenous reserve food materials: Besides carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, these materials also possess some amount of nitrogen. Protein granules are the solid forms and amino acids are the liquid form of nitrogenous reserve food materials.

b. Non-nitrogenous reserve food materials: These reserve food materials contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. The proportion of hydrogen and oxygen is found to be like in water (i.e. 2:1 in H2O). They may or may not be soluble in water. They are the products of photosynthesis e. g. starch, cellulose, sugars, inulin, glycogens, etc.

2. Secretory materials Some important chemical compounds which may not be related with nutrition are synthesized during plant metabolism. Such materials are called secretory materials. They may be of the following types:

a. Plant pigments: Phycocyanin, phycoerythrin, carotenes, fucoxanthin, flavoxanthin, lutein, chlorophyll-a, chlorophyll-b, chlorophyll-c, etc. are some colour producing substances that are secreted. These are also known as plant pigments.
b. Enzymes: These water soluble biocatalysts are the nitrogenous secretory products. c. Nectar: It is secreted by the glands known as nectaries.
3. Excretory materials Excretory materials are the by-products obtained during plant metabolism which are of useless to plants. Such excretory products are given below:

a. Alkaloids: These excretory compounds are composed of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen and occur in association with organic acids in various plant parts. For example, Quinine, nicotine, morphine, atropine, daturine, etc.
b. Organic acids: These are the outcome of various chemical processes in living cells. For example, citric acid, tartaric acid, oxalic acid, malic acid, etc.
c. Gums: These are the products obtained after the decomposition of cellulose (cell wall) which is soluble in water. They swell up in water forming a viscous mass.
d. Resins: Resins are solid, brittle, non-volatile complex substances found in various parts of plants.
e. Tannins: Tannins are non-nitrogenous, complex compounds, commonly found in unripe fruits. It is actually found dissolved in the cell sap of parenchymatous cells.
f. Essential oils: The essential oils are found in fruits, flowers, and glandular leaves of plants such as lemon, Eucalyptus, etc.
g. Latex: Latex is an emulsion of matrix in watery fluid. Starch grains, sugars, proteins, enzymes and alkaloids are dissolved in this fluid.
h. Mineral crystals: Mineral crystals are present in parenchymatous cells of several plants in the form of silica crystals, calcium carbonate crystals, calcium oxalate crystals, etc.
